french-basics.title: French Foundations — Learn French the Smart Way
french-basics.summary: A fast, visual intro to French for study abroad: pronunciation, le/la, verbs, accents and how to reach A1 quickly.

slides.title: Welcome to French!
points: French opens study in France, Belgium, Switzerland & Québec (Canada).
DELF/DALF, TCF and TEF are accepted for study & immigration.
This lesson covers the foundations + a smart learning plan.
Learn here, then use our French course, flashcards & AI tutor.
slides.tip: 20 minutes a day, every day — that's the secret.

slides.title: Accents & special letters
points: é (accent aigu), è/à (grave), ê (circonflexe), ç (cedilla), ë (tréma).
Accents change sound and meaning: ou (or) vs où (where).
ç sounds like 's' (français = 'fronsay').
Accents matter — don't skip them.

slides.title: Pronunciation basics
points: Final consonants are usually SILENT (Paris = 'paree').
'r' is throaty; 'u' is rounded (say 'ee' with lips forward).
Nasal sounds: on, an, in, un (air through the nose).
'ch' = 'sh' (chat = 'sha'); 'j' = soft 'zh'.

slides.title: Survival phrases
points: Bonjour — Hello.  Au revoir — Goodbye.
Merci — Thanks.  S'il vous plaît — Please.
Excusez-moi — Excuse me.  Pardon — Sorry.
Parlez-vous anglais? — Do you speak English?

slides.title: le, la, les — noun gender
points: Nouns are masculine (le) or feminine (la); plural = les.
Before a vowel, le/la become l' (l'ami, l'université).
Learn the article WITH the noun.
Endings hint: -tion/-té → feminine; -age/-ment → masculine.
slides.warn: Gender affects adjectives and agreement — memorise it early.

slides.title: Numbers (watch 70–99!)
points: 1–10: un, deux, trois, quatre, cinq, six, sept, huit, neuf, dix.
70 = soixante-dix (sixty-ten), 80 = quatre-vingts (four-twenties).
90 = quatre-vingt-dix (four-twenty-ten). Yes, really. 😅
Belgium/Switzerland use simpler septante, huitante, nonante.

slides.title: Subject pronouns & 'you'
points: je (I), tu (you-informal), il/elle (he/she).
nous (we), vous (you-formal/plural), ils/elles (they).
Use 'vous' with strangers and in formal settings.
Use 'tu' with friends, family, classmates.

slides.title: Key verbs: être & avoir
points: être (to be): je suis, tu es, il est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils sont.
avoir (to have): j'ai, tu as, il a, nous avons, vous avez, ils ont.
These two power most sentences — memorise them.
'Je suis étudiant' = I'm a student. 'J'ai 20 ans' = I'm 20.
slides.tip: In French you 'have' your age: 'J'ai vingt ans' = literally 'I have 20 years'.

slides.title: Regular -er verbs
points: Most verbs end in -er (parler, aimer, habiter).
Drop -er, add: -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent.
je parle, tu parles, il parle, nous parlons, vous parlez.
Master -er verbs and you can say a LOT.

slides.title: Asking questions
points: Easiest: add 'Est-ce que…' before a statement.
'Est-ce que tu parles français?' = Do you speak French?
Or just raise your intonation: 'Tu parles français?'
Question words: où, quand, comment, pourquoi, combien.

slides.title: Train your ear
points: Watch French shows with subtitles; try 'Easy French' on YouTube.
Listen to slow-French podcasts daily.
Shadow sentences aloud to fix the accent.
Use our AI tutor & natural voice for real French.

slides.title: Common beginner mistakes
points: Pronouncing silent final consonants.
Forgetting accents (they change meaning).
Mixing le/la genders.
Translating English word order directly.

slides.title: French exams for study abroad
points: DELF (A1–B2) & DALF (C1–C2): lifelong diplomas for study.
TCF: Campus France, Québec immigration, citizenship.
TEF: Canadian immigration (Express Entry).
Most French degrees want B2; Campus France guides the level.

slides.title: On y va — let's go!
points: You've got the foundations: accents, gender, key verbs, questions.
Next: open the French course (Learn tab) and flashcards.
Take the French placement test and practise speaking.
Bonne chance! 🎉
slides.tip: Open Languages → French to start your A1 course now.

slides.title: Negation: ne...pas & Beyond
points: Basic negation: ne + verb + pas (Je ne parle pas français)
Other negations: ne...jamais (never), ne...rien (nothing), ne...plus (no longer)
Double negation rare—use one negation per clause (Je ne vais jamais, not *ne jamais pas)
In informal speech, ne often drops (Je parle pas = Je ne parle pas)

example.label: Negation types
example.text: Je ne suis jamais fatigué (I am never tired) | Je ne veux rien (I want nothing) | Je ne vais plus au lycée (I no longer go to school)

slides.tip: Learn negations early—essential for saying what you DON'T do, which is 50% of A1 conversation.

slides.title: Questions: Three Ways to Ask
points: Intonation: statement with rising tone (Tu parles français? — casual)
Inversion: verb + subject (Parles-tu français? — formal, written)
Est-ce que: 'Is it that...' (Est-ce que tu parles français? — neutral, spoken)

example.label: Same question, three ways
example.text: Tu habites où? | Où habites-tu? | Où est-ce que tu habites? (Where do you live?)

slides.tip: For A1, master est-ce que—it's the safest structure and most used in speech.

slides.title: Days, Months & Time Expressions
points: Days: lundi, mardi, mercredi, jeudi, vendredi, samedi, dimanche (not capitalized)
Months: janvier, février, mars, avril, mai, juin, juillet, août, septembre, octobre, novembre, décembre
Dates: 'le 5 mai' (May 5th) or '5 mai 2026'; 'le premier janvier' (1st is special)
Time of day: le matin (morning), l'après-midi (afternoon), le soir (evening), la nuit (night)

example.label: Date & time usage
example.text: Je suis né le 12 juin. | Le meeting est lundi matin. | Nous avons un examen en décembre.

slides.tip: Practice saying dates aloud—crucial for introductions, schedules, and formal contexts.

slides.title: Food, Drinks & Ordering at Café
points: Key items: eau (water), café (coffee), thé (tea), pain (bread), fromage (cheese), viande (meat), légume (vegetable)
Ordering: 'Je voudrais... (I would like...)', 'Un café, s'il vous plaît (formal)', 'Un café, s'il te plaît (informal)'
Asking about food: 'Qu'est-ce qu'il y a? (What is there?)', 'C'est quoi? (What is it?)'
Allergies/preferences: 'Je suis végétarien(ne)', 'Je n'aime pas...', 'Je suis allergique à...'

example.label: At a café
example.text: Serveur: Qu'est-ce que tu prends? | Toi: Je voudrais un café au lait et une croissant, s'il vous plaît. | Serveur: Tout de suite!

slides.tip: Food vocabulary extends quickly—start with 10 common items, then learn to describe flavors and textures.

slides.title: Directions & Location Prepositions
points: Directions: à gauche (left), à droite (right), tout droit (straight), derrière (behind), devant (in front)
Location: près de (near), loin de (far from), en face de (opposite), à côté de (next to), entre (between)
Asking directions: 'Où est...? (Where is...?)', 'Comment aller à...? (How to get to...?)', 'Quelle est la route pour...?'
Responses: 'C'est par là (It's that way)', 'Vous continuez tout droit (You continue straight)'

example.label: Asking & giving directions
example.text: — Pardon, où est la gare? | — La gare est à côté de la mairie, près du pont. Continuez tout droit, puis tournez à gauche.

slides.tip: Learn compass directions (nord, sud, est, ouest) and common city landmarks—bridges, stations, squares.

slides.title: Near Future: aller + Infinitive
points: Form: aller (conjugated) + infinitive verb (Je vais partir = I am going to leave)
Conjugation: je vais, tu vas, il/elle va, nous allons, vous allez, ils/elles vont + infinitif
Use: informal, spoken plans (often preferred over future tense in A1)
Negation: Je ne vais pas partir (I am not going to leave); Je vais ne pas partir = same meaning

example.label: Near future plans
example.text: Je vais étudier ce soir. | Vous allez visiter Paris demain? | Ils ne vont pas venir à la fête.

slides.tip: Near future is THE way French speakers talk about plans—use it constantly in conversation.
